label: def:sysnode
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:sysnode}
  A {\em system node} on the triple $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{U},\mathcal{Y})$ of Hilbert spaces is a~linear operator ${\left[\begin{smallmatrix}A\&B\\C\&D\end{smallmatrix}\right]}$ with $A\&B:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U}\supset\operatorname{dom}(A\&B)\to \mathcal{X}$, $C\&D:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U}\supset\operatorname{dom}(C\&D)\to \mathcal{Y}$ satisfying the following conditions:
                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                            
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph{*})]
    \item $A\&B$ is closed.
    \item $C\&D\in \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{b}}(\operatorname{dom} (A\&B),\mathcal{Y})$.
    \item\label{def:sysnode3} For all $u\in \mathcal{U}$, there exists some $x\in \mathcal{X}$ with $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in \operatorname{dom}(A\&B)$.
    \item The main operator $A$ is the generator of a~strongly continuous semigroup $\mathfrak{A}(\cdot)\colon
      {\mathbb{R}}_{\ge 0}\to \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{b}}(\mathcal{X})$ on $\mathcal{X}$.
  \end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: System node

label: def:traj
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:traj}
Let ${\left[\begin{smallmatrix}A\& B\\C\& D\end{smallmatrix}\right]}$ be a~system node  on $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{U},\mathcal{Y})$, and let $T\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}$.\\
A {\em classical trajectory} of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,T]$ is a triple
\[
(x(\cdot),u(\cdot),y(\cdot))\,\in\,\mathrm{C}^{1}([0,T];\mathcal{X})\times \mathrm{C}([0,T];\mathcal{U})\times \mathrm{C}([0,T];\mathcal{Y}),
\]
which for all $t\in[0,T]$ satisfies \eqref{eq:ODEnode}.\\
A {\em generalized trajectory} of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,T]$ is a~limit
 of classical trajectories of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,T]$ in the topology of $\mathrm{C}([0,T];\mathcal{X})\times \mathrm{L}^{2}([0,T];\mathcal{U})\times \mathrm{L}^{2}([0,T];\mathcal{Y})$.\\
Further, we call 
\[
(x(\cdot),u(\cdot),y(\cdot))\,\in\,\mathrm{C}^{1}({\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0};\mathcal{X})\times \mathrm{C}({\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0};\mathcal{U})\times \mathrm{C}({\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0};\mathcal{Y})
\]
a~classical/generalized trajectory of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on ${\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0}$, if, for all $T\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}$, the restriction of $(x(\cdot),u(\cdot),y(\cdot))$ to $[0,T]$ is a~classical/generalized trajectory of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,T]$.

name: Classical/generalized trajectories

label: prop:solex
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:solex}
Let ${\left[\begin{smallmatrix}A\& B\\C\& D\end{smallmatrix}\right]}$ be a~system node  on $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{U},\mathcal{Y})$, $T\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}$, and
\[x_0\in \mathcal{X},\quad u(\cdot)\in \mathrm{W}^{2,1}([0,t];\mathcal{U})\;\text{ s.t.\ }\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x_0\\u(0)\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in \operatorname{dom} (A\&B).\]
Then there exist
$x(\cdot)\,\in\,\mathrm{C}^{1}([0,t];\mathcal{X})$ with $x(0)=x_0$, and $y(\cdot)\in \mathrm{C}([0,t];\mathcal{Y})$, such that $(x(\cdot),u(\cdot),y(\cdot))$ is a~classical trajectory
of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,T]$.

label: rem:dissall
title: Remark
body_md:
\label{rem:dissall}
   Assume the framework of Definition~\ref{def:dissineq}, and assume that $(x(\cdot),u(\cdot),y(\cdot))$ is a~classical trajectory of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,T]$. Then, for all $t_0,t_1\in[0,T]$ with $t_0\leq t_1$, it holds that
\[\mathcal{S}(x(t_1))-\mathcal{S}(x(t_0))+ \int_{t_0}^{t_1}s\bigl(y(t),u(t)\bigr)\mathop{\frac{\text{\normalfont d}}{\text{\normalfont d}t}}\geq0.\]
For $t_0=t_1$, this is obvious. If $t_0<t_1$, the statement follows from the definition of dissipativity together with the fact that
   $(\tilde{x}(\cdot),\tilde{u}(\cdot),\tilde{y}(\cdot))$ with $\tilde{x}(t)=x(t+t_0)$, $\tilde{u}(t)=u(t+t_0)$, $\tilde{y}(t)=y(t+t_0)$, $t\in[0,t_1-t_0]$, is a~classical trajectory of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,t_1-t_0]$.

label: prop:domS
title: Proposition
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Assume that $x\in \mathcal{V}$. Then there exists some $u_0\in\mathcal{U}$ with $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x_0\\u_0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\operatorname{dom}(A\&B)$. Let $u(\cdot):[0,1]\to\mathcal{U}$ be the constant function $u(\cdot)\equiv u_0$. By Proposition~\ref{prop:solex} there exist $x(\cdot)\in\mathrm{C}^{1}([0,1];\mathcal{X})$ and $y(\cdot)\in\mathrm{C}([0,1];\mathcal{Y})$, such that $(x(\cdot),u(\cdot),y(\cdot))$ is a classical trajectory of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,1]$ with $x(0)=x_0$. In particular, $x_0\in\operatorname{dom}(\mathcal{S})$. We next show that $\mathcal{S}$ is bounded on $\mathcal{V}$: Without loss of generality, we assume that $\mathcal{S}$ is semi-bounded from below (otherwise consider $-\mathcal{S}$). Consider the embedding $\iota:\mathcal{V}\to\operatorname{dom}(\mathcal{S})$. Closedness of $\mathcal{S}$ and the fact that $\mathcal{V}$ is complete implies that the graph of $\iota$ is closed. Then the closed graph theorem \cite[Thm.~7.9]{Alt16} gives $\iota\in\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{b}}(\mathcal{V},\operatorname{dom}(\mathcal{S}))$. That is, for chosing $\lambda\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\ge 0}$ such that the mapping in \eqref{eq:formnorm} (with ``$\pm=+$'') defines a norm on $\operatorname{dom}(\mathcal{S})$, there exists $C\ge 0$ such that
\[
\forall\,x\in\mathcal{V}:\quad 0\leq \mathcal{S}(x) + \lambda \norm{x}_{\mathcal{X}}^{2} \le C\,\norm{x}_{\mathcal{V}}^{2}.
\]
This immediately implies that \eqref{eq:SVbnd} holds for $c=\max\{\lambda,C\}$.

label: prop:domScont
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:domScont}
Under the assumptions of Definition~\ref{def:dissineq}, let $(x(\cdot),u(\cdot),y(\cdot))$ be a generalized trajectory of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,T]$ with $x(\cdot)\in\mathrm{C}([0,T];\operatorname{dom}(\mathcal{S}))$. Then the following statements hold:
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph{*})]
\item \eqref{eq:dissL2} and \eqref{eq:dissrate} hold for $K\&L\in\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{b}}(\mathcal{W};\mathcal{Z})$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}\,\ref{item:dissineq4}.
\item $\mathcal{S}(x(\cdot))\in\mathrm{W}^{1,1}([0,T])$.
\item The dissipation inequality \eqref{eq:dissineq_inf} holds.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph{*})]
\item Let $(x(\cdot),u(\cdot),y(\cdot))$ be a~generalized trajectory of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,T]$. Consider a `mollifier sequence' $(\alpha_n)_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}$ in $\mathrm{C}^\infty({\mathbb{R}})$, see Definition~\ref{def:molli}, and consider the 
convolutions $x_n(\cdot)$, $u_n(\cdot)$ and $y_n(\cdot)$ as in \eqref{eq:conxuy}.
Then Lemma~\ref{lem:mollconv} yields that, for all $n\in{\mathbb{N}}$, the restriction of
\[\big(x_n(\cdot),u_n(\cdot),y_n(\cdot)\big)\]
to $[0,T-1/n]$ is a~smooth classical trajectory of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,T-1/n]$. Hence, by Remark~\ref{rem:dissineq}\,\ref{rem:dissineq2}, we have, for all $n\in{\mathbb{N}}$, $T_f\in[0,T-1/n]$,
\[\mathcal{S}(x_n(T_f))-\mathcal{S}(x_n(0))+ \int_0^{T_f}s\bigl(y_n(t),u_n(t)\bigr)\mathop{\frac{\text{\normalfont d}}{\text{\normalfont d}t}}=\int_0^{T-1/n}\norm*{K\&L\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x_n(t)\\u_n(t)\end{smallmatrix}\right)}_\mathcal{Z}^2\mathop{\frac{\text{\normalfont d}}{\text{\normalfont d}t}}.\]
Now taking the limit $n\to\infty$, we obtain from Lemma~\ref{lem:mollconv} (with $\widetilde{X}=\operatorname{dom}(\mathcal{S})$) that the right hand side of the above equation converges. In particular, the restriction of $K\&L\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x(\cdot)\\u(\cdot)\end{smallmatrix}\right)$ to $[0,T_f)$ is in $\mathrm{L}^{2}$ with
\begin{multline*}
\forall\,T_f\in[0,T):\quad \mathcal{S}(x(T_f))-\mathcal{S}(x(0))+ \int_0^{T_f}s\bigl(y(t),u(t)\bigr)\mathop{\frac{\text{\normalfont d}}{\text{\normalfont d}t}}\\=\norm*{K\&L\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x(\cdot)\\u(\cdot)\end{smallmatrix}\right)}_{\mathrm{L}^{2}([0,T_f];\mathcal{Z})}^2.
\end{multline*}
Invoking that $x(\cdot)$ is continuous on $[0,T]$ as a~mapping to $\operatorname{dom}(\mathcal{S})$, the limit $T_f\nearrow T$ leads to \eqref{eq:dissL2} and \eqref{eq:dissrate}.
\item 
By using the already proven part, we obtain that, for
\[z(\cdot):=K\&L\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x(\cdot)\\u(\cdot)\end{smallmatrix}\right),\]
it holds that
\[\forall\, T_f\in[0,T]:\quad \mathcal{S}(x(T_f))=\mathcal{S}(x(0))- \int_0^{T_f}s\bigl(y(t),u(t)\bigr)\mathop{\frac{\text{\normalfont d}}{\text{\normalfont d}t}}+\int_0^{T_f}\norm{z(t)}_{\mathcal{Z}}^2\mathop{\frac{\text{\normalfont d}}{\text{\normalfont d}t}}.\]
The right hand side is, because of square integrability of $u(\cdot)$, $y(\cdot)$ and $z(\cdot)$ weakly differentiable with integrable derivative (equivalently, it is absolutely continuous), i.e.,
$\mathcal{S}(x(\cdot))\in\mathrm{W}^{1,1}([0,T])$.
\item This is a~direct consequence of the first statement in this proposition.
\end{enumerate}

label: eq:Lurebnd
title: Proof
body_md:
In the following, the lower-case Roman numerals without primes refer to the corresponding statements in Theorem~\ref{thm:main}. Our present result is established once we prove the following implications under the additional assumption of bounded storage function:
\[
\begin{array}{cccccccc}
\text{\ref{item:dissineq1}}&\Leftrightarrow&\text{\ref{item:dissineq1bnd}}&\Leftrightarrow&\text{\ref{item:dissineq5bnd}}\\
\text{\ref{item:dissineq3}}&\Rightarrow&\text{\ref{item:dissineq2bnd}}&\Rightarrow&\text{\ref{item:dissineq3bnd}}&\Rightarrow&\text{\ref{item:dissineq3}}\\
\text{\ref{item:dissineq4}}&\Leftrightarrow&\text{\ref{item:dissineq4bnd}.}
\end{array}\]
Let us first show the first line: The equivalence between \ref{item:dissineq1bnd} and \ref{item:dissineq1} is immediate, as they state exactly the same assertion. Since classical trajectories are generalized trajectories, we further have that \ref{item:dissineq5bnd} implies \ref{item:dissineq1bnd}. Since, our assumption on $\mathcal{S}$ gives $\operatorname{dom}(\mathcal{S})=\mathcal{X}$, the implication ``\ref{item:dissineq1bnd}$\Rightarrow$\ref{item:dissineq5bnd}'' follows from Proposition~\ref{prop:domScont}.\\
For the remaining parts, we first observe that the boundedness of $\mathcal{S}$ implies that $\widetilde{P}$ from Theorem~\ref{thm:main} belongs to $\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{b}}(\mathcal{X})$. Consequently, we have $\widetilde{P}=P$, a fact that will be used in the sequel.\\
\ref{item:dissineq3}$\Rightarrow$\ref{item:dissineq2bnd}: This follows from the fact that $\mathcal{W}$ is a core of $A\&B$, see Lemma~\ref{eq:Vcore}.\\
\ref{item:dissineq2bnd}$\Rightarrow$\ref{item:dissineq3bnd}: A straightforward continuity argument yields this implication.\\
\ref{item:dissineq3bnd}$\Rightarrow$\ref{item:dissineq3}:
This follows from $\mathcal{W}\subset\operatorname{dom}(A\&B)$.\\
It remains to prove the equivalence between \ref{item:dissineq4} and \ref{item:dissineq4bnd}. Since $\mathcal{W}\subset\operatorname{dom}(A\&B)$, we have that \ref{item:dissineq4bnd} implies \ref{item:dissineq4}. On the other hand, assume that \ref{item:dissineq4} holds. Then, by using $P=\widetilde{P}\in\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{b}}(\mathcal{X})$,
there exists a~Hilbert space $\mathcal{Z}$ and some $K\&L\in \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{b}}(\mathcal{V},\mathcal{Z})$ with dense range, such that, for all $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\mathcal{W}$,
\begin{equation}
    \label{eq:Lurebnd}
    2\operatorname{Re}\scprod*{{P}x}{A\&B \left(\begin{smallmatrix}x\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)}_{\mathcal{X}}+s\left({C\&D\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)},u\right)=\norm{K\&L\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)}_\mathcal{Z}^2.
    \end{equation}
Then boundedness of $P$ yields that there exists some $M>0$, such that, for all $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\mathcal{W}$,
\[\norm{K\&L\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)}_\mathcal{Z}^2\leq \norm{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)}_{\operatorname{dom}(A\&B)}^2.\]
The density of $\mathcal{W}$ in $\operatorname{dom}(A\&B)$ (see Lemma~\ref{eq:Vcore}) implies that $K\&L$ extends to a bounded operator from $\operatorname{dom}(A\&B)$ to $\mathcal{Z}$. Clearly, its range is dense as well. Then a~continuity argument yields that \eqref{eq:Lurebnd} holds for all $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\operatorname{dom}(A\&B)$. Thus, \ref{item:dissineq4bnd} holds, and the proof is finished.

title: Proof
body_md:
Consider an infinite-time stabilizing state feedback $F\&G\in\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{b}}(\operatorname{dom}(A\&B))$. Let $x_0\in\mathcal{X}$. Now driving the closed-loop system
\eqref{eq:extsysnode}, $u(\cdot)=z(\cdot)+v(\cdot)$, with $v(\cdot)=0$,
we obtain that there exists a~solution \[\left(x(\cdot),0,\left(\begin{smallmatrix}y(\cdot)\\z(\cdot)\end{smallmatrix}\right)\right)\text{ with $x(0)=x_0$ and $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}y(\cdot)\\z(\cdot)\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\mathrm{L}^{2}({\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0};\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{U})$}.\] 
 Since
$(x(\cdot),{z(\cdot)},{y(\cdot)})$ is then a~generalized solution of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on ${\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0}$, the first statement holds. Further, infinite-time well-posedness of the closed-loop yields that the closed-loop system (again driven by $v(\cdot)$) has the property that, for all $x_0\in\mathcal{X}$, the output fulfills
\[\norm*{\left(\begin{smallmatrix}y(\cdot)\\z(\cdot)\end{smallmatrix}\right)}_{\mathrm{L}^{2}({\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0};\mathcal{Y}\times\mathcal{U})}\leq M \norm{x_0}_\mathcal{X}.\]
Now invoking that, by $v(\cdot)=0$, we have $z(\cdot)=u(\cdot)$, we obtain that the desired estimate holds.
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
\
    \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph{*})]
        \item Our notion in Definition~\ref{def:stabilizable} differs slightly from the classical
finite-dimensional one (see, e.g., \cite{TrentelmanStoorvogelHautus2001}), where
stabilizability means that there exists a (static) state feedback $u(t)=Fx(t)+v(t)$
such that the closed-loop matrix $A+BF$ is Hurwitz (equivalently, all unstable modes
are controllable).

By contrast, Definition~\ref{def:stabilizable} employs an \emph{admissible} state
feedback of the form $F\&G$ and requires that the closed-loop interconnection defines
an \emph{infinite-time well-posed} system node. In particular, this notion permits semisimple modes on the imaginary axis that are simultaneously uncontrollable and unobservable. Such modes are excluded by the standard finite-dimensional definition.
\item If the system is internally passive, then the output feedback $u(t)=-y(t)+v(t)$ renders the closed-loop system infinite-time well-posed; see \cite[Thm.~4.2]{HastirPaunonen2025}. In particular, every internally passive system is state-feedback stabilizable (take the admissible feedback $F\&G=-\,(C\&D)$ so that $u(\cdot)=-y(\cdot)+v(\cdot)$).

As a consequence, the class of port-Hamiltonian systems governed by system nodes (as treated in \cite{PhilippReisSchaller2025}) is state-feedback stabilizable.                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                
    \end{enumerate}

label: thm:costfun
title: Theorem
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\
For brevity, we adopt the following convention: a ``generalized trajectory'' means a generalized trajectory of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on ${\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0}$.
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph{*})]
\item Nonnegativity of $\mathcal{S}$ follows directly from nonnegativity of $s(\cdot,\cdot)$. Further, it follows from Lemma~\ref{lem:iobnd} that $\mathrm{Val}(x_0)\in{\mathbb{R}}$ for all  $x_0\in\mathcal{X}$.\\
The statement that $\mathcal{S}$ is a~bounded quadratic form  will be proven in several steps.\\
{\em Step~1}: We show that $\mathrm{Val}(\lambda x_0)=|\lambda|^2\mathrm{Val}(x_0)$ for all $x_0\in\mathcal{X}$, $\lambda\in{\mathbb{C}}$. The statement is clear for $\lambda=0$, so we can assume that $\lambda\neq0$ in the following.\\
Let $x_0\in\mathcal{X}$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Then, by Lemma~\ref{lem:iobnd} and the definition of the value function, there exists a~generalized trajectory $(x(\cdot),u(\cdot),y(\cdot))$ with $x(0)=x_0$ and 
\[\mathcal{J}\bigl(y(\cdot),u(\cdot)\bigr)\leq \mathrm{Val}(x_0)+\frac{\varepsilon}{|\lambda|^2}.\]
Using that $(\lambda x(\cdot),\lambda u(\cdot),\lambda y(\cdot))$ is a~generalized trajectory with $\lambda x(0)=\lambda x_0$, we obtain, by 
quadraticity of $s$,
\begin{multline*}
 \mathrm{Val}(\lambda x_0)\leq \mathcal{J}(\lambda x(\cdot),\lambda u(\cdot))=|\lambda|^2\mathcal{J}( y(\cdot),u(\cdot))
  = |\lambda|^2\,\mathcal{J}(y(\cdot),u(\cdot))\\
  \leq |\lambda|^2\left(\mathrm{Val}(x_0)+\frac{\varepsilon}{|\lambda|^2}\right)
  =|\lambda|^2\mathrm{Val}(x_0)+\varepsilon.
\end{multline*}
Since the latter holds for all $\varepsilon>0$, we have
$\mathrm{Val}(\lambda x_0)\leq |\lambda|^2 \mathcal{S}(x_0)$.
Applying this with $x_0$ replaced by $\lambda x_0$ and with the factor $1/\lambda$ gives the reverse inequality, hence $\mathrm{Val}(\lambda x_0)=|\lambda|^2\mathrm{Val}(x_0)$.\\
{\em Step~2}: We show the parallelogram identity
\[
  \forall\,x_{0,1},x_{0,2}\in\mathcal{X}:\quad \mathrm{Val}(x_{0,1}+x_{0,2})+\mathrm{Val}(x_{0,1}-x_{0,2})
  =2\mathrm{Val}(x_{0,1})+2\mathrm{Val}(x_{0,2})
  .
\]
Let $x_{0,1},x_{0,2}\in\mathcal{X}$ and $\varepsilon>0$. Then there exist 
generalized trajectories $(x_i(\cdot),u_i(\cdot),y_i(\cdot))$ with $x_i(0)=x_{0,i}$ such that
\[
\mathcal{J}\bigl(y_i(\cdot),u_i(\cdot)\bigr)\le\mathrm{Val}(x_{0,i})+\frac{\varepsilon}{4},
  \qquad i=1,2.
\]
Clearly, the sums and differences
\[
  (x_\pm(\cdot),u_\pm(\cdot),y_\pm(\cdot)):=\bigl(x_1(\cdot)\pm x_2(\cdot),\;u_1(\cdot)\pm u_2(\cdot),\;y_1(\cdot)\pm y_2(\cdot)\bigr)
\]
are generalized trajectories with initial states $x_{0,1}\pm x_{0,2}$. Since $s$ is quadratic,
we have the integrand-level parallelogram identity, and hence
\[
  \mathcal{J}\bigl(y_+,u_+\bigr)+\mathcal{J}\bigl(y_-,u_-\bigr)
=2\mathcal{J}\bigl(y_1,u_1\bigr)+2\mathcal{J}\bigl(y_2,u_2\bigr).
\]
Therefore,
\[
  \mathrm{Val}(x_{0,1}+x_{0,2})+\mathrm{Val}(x_{0,1}-x_{0,2})
  \le2\,\mathrm{Val}(x_{0,1})+2\mathrm{Val}(x_{0,2})+\varepsilon.
\]
Since $\varepsilon>0$ is arbitrary, we obtain
\[
  \mathrm{Val}(x_{0,1}+x_{0,2})+\mathrm{Val}(x_{0,1}-x_{0,2})
  \le2\,\mathrm{Val}(x_{0,1})+2\mathrm{Val}(x_{0,2}).
\]
For the reverse inequality, set $\tilde x_{0,1}:=\tfrac12(x_{0,1}+x_{0,2})$ and 
$\tilde x_{0,2}:=\tfrac12(x_{0,1}-x_{0,2})$. Applying the previous estimate to 
$\tilde x_{0,1},\tilde x_{0,2}$ and using Step~1 with $\lambda=\tfrac12$, we get
\begin{multline*}
  2\mathrm{Val}(x_{0,1})+2\mathrm{Val}(x_{0,2})
  =4\mathrm{Val}(\tilde x_{0,1})+4\,\mathrm{Val}(\tilde x_{0,2})\\
  \le\mathrm{Val}(x_{0,1}+x_{0,2})+\mathrm{Val}(x_{0,1}-x_{0,2}),
\end{multline*}
which proves the parallelogram identity.\\
{\em Step~3:} We conclude that $\mathrm{Val}$ is a quadratic form. Indeed, Steps~1-2 verify the hypotheses of \cite[Thm.~1]{Kurepa1965QSF}; hence, by that theorem, \eqref{eq:hsesq} is a~sesquilinear form. Thus $\mathrm{Val}:\mathcal{X}\to{\mathbb{R}}$ is a quadratic form.\\
{\em Step~4:} We show that $\mathrm{Val}$ is a bounded quadratic form. It can be concluded from  Lemma~\ref{lem:iobnd} that, for $M$ as in that lemma, 
\[\forall\, x_0\in\mathcal{X}\text{ with }\norm{x_0}_\mathcal{X}\leq 1:\quad\mathrm{Val}(x_0)\leq M\,\norm*{\left[\begin{smallmatrix}Q & S\\S 
  \setcounter{i}{1} 
  \striche={\ast} 
  \loop 
  \ifnum\value{i}<1 
  \striche=\expandafter{\the\expandafter\striche\ast} 
  \stepcounter{i} 
  \repeat 
  ^{\the\striche} 
 & R\end{smallmatrix}\right]}.\] Hence, by using that $\mathrm{Val}$ is quadratic, we have \[\forall\, x_0\in\mathcal{X}:\quad\mathrm{Val}(x_0)\leq M\,\norm*{\left[\begin{smallmatrix}Q & S\\S 
  \setcounter{i}{1} 
  \striche={\ast} 
  \loop 
  \ifnum\value{i}<1 
  \striche=\expandafter{\the\expandafter\striche\ast} 
  \stepcounter{i} 
  \repeat 
  ^{\the\striche} 
 & R\end{smallmatrix}\right]}\,\norm{x_0}_\mathcal{X}^2.\]
\item 
Assume that $(x(\cdot),u(\cdot),y(\cdot))$ is a~classical trajectory on $[0,T]$, $T>0$. 
We essentially follow the argument of the corresponding finite-dimensional proof in \cite{Will71a}. 
For $\varepsilon>0$, let $({x}_1(\cdot),{u}_1(\cdot),{y}_1(\cdot))$
be a generalized solution with ${x}_1(0)=x(T)$ and 
\[
\mathcal{J}\bigl({y}_1(\cdot),{u}_1(\cdot)\bigr)\le\mathrm{Val}(x(T))+{\varepsilon}.
\]
Now consider the \emph{concatenation} of the two trajectories, defined by
\[
(\tilde x(t),\tilde u(t),\tilde y(t))=
\begin{cases}
(x(t),u(t),y(t)), & 0\le t\le T,\\
\bigl(x_1(t-T),u_1(t-T),y_1(t-T)\bigr), & t> T,
\end{cases}
\]
Then $(\tilde x(\cdot),\tilde u(\cdot),\tilde y(\cdot))$ is a~generalized trajectory with $\tilde u(\cdot)\in\mathrm{L}^{2}({\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0};\mathcal{U})$ and $\tilde y(\cdot)\in\mathrm{L}^{2}({\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0};\mathcal{Y})$, whence
\begin{align*}
    \mathrm{Val}(x(0))&=\mathrm{Val}(\tilde{x}(0))\leq \mathcal{J}(\tilde{y}(\cdot),\tilde{u}(\cdot))\\&=\int_0^Ts\bigl(\tilde{y}(t),\tilde{u}(t)\bigr)\mathop{\frac{\text{\normalfont d}}{\text{\normalfont d}t}}+\int_0^\infty s\bigl(\tilde{y}(t+T),\tilde{u}(t+T)\bigr)\mathop{\frac{\text{\normalfont d}}{\text{\normalfont d}t}}\\
                                                                                                    
        &=\int_0^Ts\bigl({y}(t),{u}(t)\bigr)\mathop{\frac{\text{\normalfont d}}{\text{\normalfont d}t}}+\mathcal{J}\bigl({y}_1(\cdot),{u}_1(\cdot)\bigr)\mathop{\frac{\text{\normalfont d}}{\text{\normalfont d}t}}\\
                &\leq\int_0^Ts\bigl({y}(t),{u}(t)\bigr)\mathop{\frac{\text{\normalfont d}}{\text{\normalfont d}t}}+\mathrm{Val}(x(T))+\varepsilon.
\end{align*}
Since this holds for all $\varepsilon>0$, we can conclude that the dissipation inequality holds.
\item Let $x_0\in\mathcal{V}$, with $\mathcal{V}$ as in \eqref{eq:Vdef}. For every classical trajectory
$(x(\cdot),u(\cdot),y(\cdot))$ on ${\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0}$ with $x(0)=x_0$ we have, for all $T>0$,
\[
  0 \;\le\; \mathcal{S}(x(T))-\mathcal{S}(x_0) \;+\; \int_0^T s\bigl(y(t),u(t)\bigr)\,\mathop{\frac{\text{\normalfont d}}{\text{\normalfont d}t}}.
\]
Since $\mathcal{S}\ge0$, letting $T\to\infty$, we obtain
\[
  \mathcal{S}(x_0)\;\le\;\int_0^\infty s\bigl(y(t),u(t)\bigr)\,\mathop{\frac{\text{\normalfont d}}{\text{\normalfont d}t}}.
\]
Taking the infimum over all trajectories with $x(0)=x_0$ yields
\[
  \mathcal{S}(x_0)\;\le\;\mathrm{Val}(x_0).
\]
Thus $\mathcal{S}$ is bounded above by $\mathrm{Val}$ on $\mathcal{V}$. By density of $\mathcal{V}$ in $\mathcal{X}$
(and nonnegativity of $\mathcal{S}$), the inequality in fact holds for all
$x_0\in\mathcal{X}$, which completes the proof.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

label: prop:xtends0
title: Proposition
body_md:
\label{prop:xtends0}
Assume the standing hypotheses of Theorem~\ref{thm:costfun}, and let
$(x(\cdot),u(\cdot),y(\cdot))$ be a generalized trajectory of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on ${\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0}$
with $x(0)=x_0$, $u(\cdot)\in\mathrm{L}^{2}({\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0};\mathcal{U})$, and $y(\cdot)\in\mathrm{L}^{2}({\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0};\mathcal{Y})$. Then
\[
  \lim_{t\to\infty} \mathrm{Val}\bigl(x(t)\bigr)=0.
\]
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
By a~simple shift, we see that 
    \[\forall\, t\in{\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0}:\quad 0\leq \mathrm{Val}(x(t))\leq \int_t^\infty s(y(\tau),u(\tau))\mathop{\mathrm{d}\tau}.\]
Then the result follows, since, by invoking that $s$ is nonnegative, Lebesgue's dominated convergence theorem gives
\[\lim_{t\to\infty}\int_t^\infty s(y(\tau),u(\tau))\mathop{\mathrm{d}\tau}=0.\]
head: environment

title: Remark
body_md:
We have seen that, under the standing assumptions of nonnegativity of the cost functional and state–feedback stabilizability, the value function is a bounded storage function with respect to the supply rate $s$. 
Boundedness implies the existence of a self-adjoint $P\in\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{b}}(\mathcal{X})$ such that 
\[
\mathrm{Val}(x_0)=\scprod{ x_0}{Px_0}_\mathcal{X}\quad\text{for all }x_0\in\mathcal{X}.
\]
Moreover, Theorem~\ref{thm:mainbnd} yields a Hilbert space $\mathcal{Z}$ and an operator $K\&L\in\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{b}}(\operatorname{dom}(A\&B);\mathcal{Z})$ with dense range such that \eqref{eq:kyp_inf_lurebnd} holds for all $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\operatorname{dom}(A\&B)$. 
Applying Proposition~\ref{prop:domScontbnd}, we obtain the following: for $K\&L\in\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{b}}(\operatorname{dom}(A\&B))$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:mainbnd}\,\ref{item:dissineq4bnd}, and for all $T>0$, every generalized solution of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,T]$ satisfies
\[
  \mathrm{Val}(x(T))-\mathrm{Val}(x(0))
  \;+\; \int_0^{T}s\bigl(y(t),u(t)\bigr)\,\mathop{\frac{\text{\normalfont d}}{\text{\normalfont d}t}}
  \;=\; \int_0^{T}\norm*{K\&L\,\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x(t)\\u(t)\end{smallmatrix}\right)}_{\mathcal{Z}}^{2}\,\mathop{\frac{\text{\normalfont d}}{\text{\normalfont d}t}}.
\]
Invoking Proposition~\ref{prop:xtends0}, which states that $\mathrm{Val}(x(t))\to 0$ as $t\to\infty$ for any generalized trajectory with $u,y\in L^2({\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0})$, we conclude that
\[
  \mathrm{Val}(x_0)\;+\;\norm*{K\&L\,\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x(\cdot)\\u(\cdot)\end{smallmatrix}\right)}_{L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0};\mathcal{Z})}^{2}
  \;=\; \mathcal{J}\bigl(y(\cdot),u(\cdot)\bigr).
\]
Hence the quantity $\norm*{K\&L\,\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x(\cdot)\\u(\cdot)\end{smallmatrix}\right)}_{L^{2}({\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0};\mathcal{Z})}^{2}$ measures the suboptimality gap of the control $u(\cdot)$ relative to the optimal cost. In particular, an optimal control exists if and only if the infinite-dimensional differential–algebraic equation
\[
  \left(\begin{smallmatrix}\dot{x}(t)\\0\end{smallmatrix}\right)
  \;=\;
  \begin{bmatrix}A\&B\\[-1mm] K\&L\end{bmatrix}\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x(t)\\u(t)\end{smallmatrix}\right),
  \qquad x(0)=x_0,
\]
admits a solution; any such solution then yields an optimal control. 
In the finite-dimensional case, this closed-loop system coincides with the classical feedback system obtained by the solution of the algebraic Riccati equation \cite{Will71a}.
head: environment
name: The optimal control

title: Remark
body_md:
In \cite{OpmeerStaffans2014,OpmeerStaffans2019}, the minimization of the cost functional
\[
\norm{u(\cdot)}_{\mathrm{L}^{2}({\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0};\mathcal{U})}^2+\norm{y(\cdot)}_{\mathrm{L}^{2}({\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0};\mathcal{Y})}^2
\]
subject to a prescribed initial value is considered. In our notation, this corresponds to a supply rate $s(\cdot,\cdot)$ as in \eqref{eq:supply_inf} with $S=0$, $R=I_\mathcal{U}$, and $Q=I_\mathcal{Y}$. One essentially obtains the same equations as in \eqref{eq:kyp_inf_lure} for this setting. On the one hand, that cost functional is more restrictive than ours; on the other hand, the class of systems is broader, as \emph{operator nodes} rather than system nodes are treated. Roughly speaking, this framework does not require the state operator $A$ to generate a strongly continuous semigroup; it suffices that $A$ be densely defined with a nonempty resolvent set (e.g., this allows one to treat the backward heat equation).

In \cite{OpmeerStaffans2014,OpmeerStaffans2019}, a frequency-domain viewpoint is adopted, and for a subdomain $\Omega$ of the resolvent set of $A$ intersected with the complex right half-plane, the output (when it belongs to $\mathrm{L}^{2}({\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0};\mathcal{Y})$) is defined via the inverse Laplace transform of the analytic continuation of
\begin{align*}
\widehat{y}:\quad\Omega&\to\mathcal{Y},\\
s&\mapsto G(s)\widehat{u}(s)+C\&D\left(\begin{smallmatrix}(sI_\mathcal{X} -A)^{-1}x_0\\0\end{smallmatrix}\right),
\end{align*}
where $\widehat{u}(\cdot)$ is the Laplace transform of $u(\cdot)$, and $G(\cdot)$ is the transfer function of ${\left[\begin{smallmatrix}A\& B\\C\& D\end{smallmatrix}\right]}$, see \cite[Sec.~4.6]{Staf05}. Indeed, by \cite[Lem.~4.7.12]{Staf05}, generalized trajectories satisfy the above frequency-domain relation. We also note that the solution concept in \cite{OpmeerStaffans2014,OpmeerStaffans2019} is considerably more general, not only because operator nodes (rather than system nodes) are treated, but also because the state trajectory need not be continuous as a map ${\mathbb{R}}_{\ge0}\to\mathcal{X}$. Moreover, no state-feedback stabilizability assumption is imposed; instead, the existence of $\mathrm{L}^{2}$-trajectories is required for a dense subspace of \(\mathcal{X}\) (which also leads to unbounded value functions).

It is important to observe that those results make essential use of the fact that the $\mathrm{L}^{2}$-norm of the input enters the cost functional. Without going into details, these results can be applied more or less directly to optimal problems \eqref{eq:optcontr} with full input weighting (that is, $R$ in \eqref{eq:supply_inf} is boundedly invertible). The case of more general cost functionals (even nonnegative ones), however, still requires additional work beyond the scope of this article.
head: environment

label: eq:Vcore
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $A$ generates a strongly continuous semigroup, it is densely defined \cite[Chap.~2, Thm.~1.4]{EngeNage00}. Hence, a~combination of \eqref{eq:ABdom} with property \ref{def:sysnode3} from Definition~\ref{def:sysnode} implies that $A\&B$ is densely defined.\\
It remains to prove that $\mathcal{W}$ is a~core of $A\&B$. Since $A$ generates a~strongly continuous semigroup, it follows from \cite[Chap.~2, Thm.~1.10]{EngeNage00} that  $\lambda I_\mathcal{X}-A$ is bijective for some $\lambda\in{\mathbb{C}}$. Consequently, the operator
\begin{align*}
    T:\quad\operatorname{dom}(A\&B)&\to \mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U},\\
    \left(\begin{smallmatrix}x\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)&\mapsto \left(\begin{smallmatrix}A\&B\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)-\lambda x\\[-1mm]\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)
\end{align*}
is bijective. It can be further seen that the inverse of $T$ fulfills
\begin{align*}
    T^{-1}:\quad\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U} &\to \operatorname{dom}(A\&B),\\
    \left(\begin{smallmatrix}x\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)&\mapsto \left(\begin{smallmatrix}(A-\lambda I_\mathcal{X})^{-1}x-(A_{-1}-\lambda I_\mathcal{X} )^{-1}Bu\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right).
\end{align*}
Now assume that $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\operatorname{dom}(A\&B)$. To prove the desired result, we have to show that there exists a~sequence $\big(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x_n\\u_n\end{smallmatrix}\right)\big)$  in $\mathcal{V}$ which converges in $\operatorname{dom}(A\&B)$ to $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Since $\operatorname{dom}(A\&B)$ is dense in $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U}$, there exists a~sequence $\big(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}z_n\\w_n\end{smallmatrix}\right)\big)$ in $\operatorname{dom}(A\&B)$ which converges in $\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{U}$ to $T\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Define
\[
\big(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x_n\\u_n\end{smallmatrix}\right)\big):=T^{-1}\big(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}z_n\\w_n\end{smallmatrix}\right)\big).\]
Then it follows immediately that $\big(\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x_n\\u_n\end{smallmatrix}\right)\big)$ converges in $\operatorname{dom}(A\&B)$ to $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x\\u\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Further, the structure of $T^{-1}$ yields that
\[\forall\,n\in{\mathbb{N}}:\quad A\&B\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x_n\\u_n\end{smallmatrix}\right)=z_n+\lambda x_n\in\mathcal{V}.\]
The latter gives $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x_n\\u_n\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in \mathcal{W}$ for all $n\in{\mathbb{N}}$,
and the result is proven.
head: environment

label: lem:smoothsol
title: Lemma
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Closedness of $\mathcal{S}$ together with smoothness of $x(\cdot)$, $u(\cdot)$ and $y(\cdot)$ yields that a~formal differentiation of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} is possible, whence, $(\dot{x}(\cdot),\dot{u}(\cdot),\dot{y}(\cdot))$ is a classical trajectory of  \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,T]$. In particular, 
\[\left(\begin{smallmatrix}\dot{x}(\cdot)\\\dot{u}(\cdot)\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\mathrm{C}([0,T];\operatorname{dom}(A\&B)),\]
and, consequently, $\dot{x}(\cdot)\in \mathrm{C}([0,T];\mathcal{V})$. This implies that $x(\cdot)\in \mathrm{C}^{1}([0,T];\mathcal{V})$, and, by \[A\&B\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x(\cdot)\\u(\cdot)\end{smallmatrix}\right)=\dot{x}(\cdot)\in \mathrm{C}([0,T];\mathcal{W}),\] we also obtain that 
\[\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x(\cdot)\\u(\cdot)\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in \mathrm{C}([0,T];\mathcal{W}).\]
head: environment

label: lem:solexsmooth
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:solexsmooth}
Let ${\left[\begin{smallmatrix}A\& B\\C\& D\end{smallmatrix}\right]}$ be a~system node  on $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{U},\mathcal{Y})$, $T\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}$, and let $\mathcal{V}$ and $\mathcal{W}$ be as in \eqref{eq:Vdef} and \eqref{eq:Wdef}.
Then, for all $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x_0\\u_0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in \mathcal{W}$, there exists 
a~classical trajectory $(x(\cdot),u(\cdot),y(\cdot))$ of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,T]$ with $x(0)=x_0$, $u(0)=u_0$, $x\in \mathrm{C}^{2}([0,t];\mathcal{X})$ and $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x(\cdot)\\u(\cdot)\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in \mathrm{C}([0,T];\mathcal{W})$.
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
Since $\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x_0\\u_0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in \mathcal{W}$, there exists some $u_0\in \mathcal{U}$, such that 
\[\left(\begin{smallmatrix}A\&B\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x_0\\u_0\end{smallmatrix}\right)\\u_1\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in\operatorname{dom}(A\&B).\]
By simple interpolation, we obtain that there exists some  
\[u(\cdot)\in \mathrm{W}^{3,1}([0,T];\mathcal{U})\;\text{ s.t.\ }u(0)=u_0\text{ and }\dot{u}(0)=u_1.\]
Then Proposition~\ref{prop:solex} implies that there exist classical trajectories $(x(\cdot),u(\cdot),y(\cdot))$, $(x_1(\cdot),\dot{u}(\cdot),y_1(\cdot))$ on $[0,T]$ with $x(0)=x_0$ and $x_1(0)=A\&B\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x_0\\u_0\end{smallmatrix}\right)$. Then {\cite[Thm.~3.8.2]{Staf05}}
gives $x_1(\cdot)=\dot{x}(\cdot)$. Hence, $x(\cdot)\in\mathrm{C}^2([0,T];\mathcal{X})$ and, by further invoking that $u(\cdot)\in \mathrm{W}^{3,1}([0,T];\mathcal{U})\subset \mathrm{C}^2([0,T];\mathcal{X})$, an application of Lemma~\ref{lem:smoothsol} leads \[x(\cdot)\in \mathrm{C}^{1}([0,T];\mathcal{V})\;\text{ and }\;\left(\begin{smallmatrix}x(\cdot)\\u(\cdot)\end{smallmatrix}\right)\in \mathrm{C}([0,t];\mathcal{W}),\] the desired result.
head: environment

label: def:molli
title: Definition
body_md:
\label{def:molli}
    By a `mollifier sequence', we mean a~sequence $(\alpha_n)_{n\in{\mathbb{N}}}$ in $\mathrm{C}^\infty({\mathbb{R}})$, such that, for all $n\in{\mathbb{N}}$,
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph{*})]
  \item $\displaystyle \int_{\mathbb{R}} \alpha_n(t)\,\mathop{\frac{\text{\normalfont d}}{\text{\normalfont d}t}} = 1$,
  \item the support of $\alpha_n $ is contained in $(-1/n,0]$,
  \item $\alpha_n(t)\ge 0 \text{ for all } t\in {\mathbb{R}}$.
\end{enumerate}
head: environment
name: Mollifier sequence

label: lem:mollconv
title: Lemma
body_md:
\label{lem:mollconv}
    Let ${\left[\begin{smallmatrix}A\& B\\C\& D\end{smallmatrix}\right]}$ be a~system node  on $(\mathcal{X},\mathcal{U},\mathcal{Y})$, let $T\in{\mathbb{R}}_{>0}$, and assume that $(x(\cdot),u(\cdot),y(\cdot))$ is a generalized trajectory of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,T]$. Consider the 
convolutions $x_n:=\alpha_n\ast x:[0,T]\to\mathcal{X}$,
$u_n:=\alpha_n\ast u:[0,T]\to\mathcal{U}$, 
$y_n:=\alpha_n\ast y:[0,T]\to\mathcal{Y}$. Then the following holds:
  \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph{*})]
 \item\label{lem:mollconv1} For all 
$n\in{\mathbb{N}}$, $(x_n(\cdot),u_n(\cdot),y_n(\cdot))$ is a~classical and infinitely often differentiable trajectory of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,T-1/n]$
\item\label{lem:mollconv2} For all $\varepsilon>0$, the restriction of $\big((x_n(\cdot),u_n(\cdot),y_n(\cdot))\big)$ to $[0,T-\varepsilon]$ converges to the restriction of $(x(\cdot),u(\cdot),y(\cdot))$ to  $[0,T-\varepsilon]$ in the topology of $\mathrm{C}([0,T-\varepsilon];\mathcal{X})\times \mathrm{L}^{2}([0,T-\varepsilon];\mathcal{U})\times \mathrm{L}^{2}([0,T-\varepsilon];\mathcal{Y})$.
\item\label{lem:mollconv3} If, moreover, for some Hilbert space $\widetilde{\mathcal{X}}\subset\mathcal{X}$, it holds
that $x(\cdot)\in\mathrm{C}([0,T];\widetilde{\mathcal{X}})$, then the sequence $(x_n(t))$ converges in $\mathcal{V}$ to $x(t)$ for all $t\in[0,T)$.  
\end{enumerate}
head: environment

title: Proof
body_md:
\
\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph{*})]
\item Smoothness of $x_n(\cdot)$, $u_n(\cdot)$ and $y_n(\cdot)$ is a~classical result, see e.g.\ \cite[Sec.~4.14]{Alt16}.
Since we have a~generalized trajectory, there exists a~sequence $(\tilde{x}_m(\cdot),\tilde{u}_m(\cdot),\tilde{y}_m(\cdot))$ which converges to $(x(\cdot),u(\cdot),y(\cdot))$ in the topology of $\mathrm{C}([0,T];\mathcal{X})\times \mathrm{L}^{2}([0,T];\mathcal{U})\times \mathrm{L}^{2}([0,T];\mathcal{Y})$. A~differentiation of the convolution integrals yields that, for all $n,m\in{\mathbb{N}}$, 
$(\alpha_n\ast\tilde{x}_m(\cdot),\alpha_n\ast\tilde{u}_m(\cdot),\alpha_n\ast\tilde{y}_m(\cdot))$ is a~classical trajectory of 
of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,T-1/n]$. Further, by \cite[Prop~4.21 \& Thm.~4.22]{Brezis2011}, we have for all $n\in{\mathbb{N}}$ that the limit $m\to\infty$
of
\[(\alpha_n\ast\tilde{x}_m(\cdot),\alpha_n\ast\tilde{u}_m(\cdot),\alpha_n\ast\tilde{y}_m(\cdot))\]
in the topology of $\mathrm{C}([0,T];\mathcal{X})\times \mathrm{L}^{2}([0,T];\mathcal{U})\times \mathrm{L}^{2}([0,T];\mathcal{Y})$ is given by $(x_n(\cdot),u_n(\cdot),y_n(\cdot))$.
Hence, for all $n\in{\mathbb{N}}$, $(x_n(\cdot),u_n(\cdot),y_n(\cdot))$ is a~generalized trajectory 
of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,T-1/n]$. Now invoking smoothness of $(x_n(\cdot),u_n(\cdot),y_n(\cdot))$ we even have that  
it is a~classical trajectory 
of \eqref{eq:ODEnode} on $[0,T-1/n]$.
\item This follows by an application of \cite[Prop~4.21 \& Thm.~4.22]{Brezis2011}.
\item This again follows from \cite[Prop~4.21]{Brezis2011}.
\end{enumerate}
